html:
The Paris Psalter is a Byzantine illuminated manuscript of the Book of Psalms, probably made in Constantinople in the mid 10th century. It is kept in the national library of France in Paris, which gives it its name.

Its fame rests on 14 full-page paintings. Most show the life of David, the supposed author of the Psalms, and others show scenes such as the crossing of the Red Sea. The style is classical: solid figures in landscapes, with personified ideas and places beside them, such as Melody sitting next to David as he plays the harp, in the manner of ancient Greek and Roman painting.

Scholars see it as a key work of the Macedonian Renaissance, the 10th-century revival of classical learning and art linked with the court of Constantine VII. Whether its painters copied a much older book or chose to revive an old style is still debated. Either way, after the end of iconoclasm, Byzantine artists looked back to the ancient world as a living model.
